title: Evaluating a source (CRAAP)
intent: formative · pattern spot-the-error / source-evaluation · judge one lens at a time
statement: You are deciding whether to cite this. Work the CRAAP test — Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose — one lens at a time, and stamp a verdict on each.

source.title: “Why Solar Will Power Everything by 2027”
source.meta: greenfuturenow.blog · no author listed · posted 2019 · no citations

items.label: Currency
items.question: recent enough?
items.verdict: A 2019 post whose 2027 forecast is already overtaken.

items.label: Relevance
items.question: the right depth?
items.verdict: On topic, but a shallow overview — relevant yet thin.

items.label: Authority
items.question: who says so?
items.verdict: No named author; a self-published blog. Authority fails.

items.label: Accuracy

items.label: Purpose

steps.title: Meet the source
steps.text: Before judging, see what you are dealing with. Work the five CRAAP lenses in order.

steps.title: C — Currency
steps.text: How recent is it, and does recency matter here? For a fast-moving topic, an overtaken forecast is a warning.

steps.title: R — Relevance
steps.text: Does it address your question at the right depth? A source can be on topic yet too shallow to use.

steps.title: A — Authority
steps.text: Who wrote it, and what makes them credible? No named author on a self-published blog is a serious problem.

steps.title: A — Accuracy
steps.text: Is it supported and verifiable? No citations means you cannot check a single claim.

steps.title: P — Purpose
steps.text: Why was it made — to inform, or to persuade and sell? Spot the bias before you trust it.

steps.title: Reach a verdict
steps.text: Weigh the five lenses together. Relevant is not the same as reliable: this one fails where it matters most.

feedForward.text: Relevant but not reliable — it fails Authority and Accuracy. Use it only to illustrate hype, and corroborate every claim with peer-reviewed or official data.
